title: Later Shu
capsule: The Later Shu (後蜀, Hòu Shǔ) was one of the Ten Kingdoms established in the Sichuan basin by Meng Zhixiang, a former Tang military governor who declared independence in 934 following the collapse of the Later Tang kingdom. His son Meng Chang (r. 934–965) proved an effective ruler who patronised literature and the arts, overseeing a period of relative stability and prosperity in the Chengdu plain compared to the endemic warfare elsewhere in China. Song forces under Wang Quanbin conquered the kingdom in 965 in a campaign of sixty-six days, capturing Meng Chang and ending Sichuan's independent status as the Song empire achieved control of the Chinese heartland.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. The Later Shu's territorial extent in the Sichuan basin is well bounded by geography and well documented in Song-era sources; frontier zones in Hanzhong and Yunnan are less precisely delimited.
